difficultyRationale: Requires reading a small multi-concern method and separating true reasons-to-change from surface details like annotations or construction style.
explanation: The method interleaves validation, persistence, email delivery and audit logging — four concerns that change for different reasons and are owned by different stakeholders (product/validation rules, DBAs/schema, marketing/email copy, compliance/audit requirements). That mixture, not the method count or framework choice, is what SRP flags.

options.text: The class is annotated `@Service`, and Spring stereotypes should only ever be applied to classes with exactly one public method — `register` already satisfies that, so there is no SRP concern here.
options.explanation: A single public method says nothing about SRP; the question is how many unrelated reasons-to-change are folded inside that one method's body, and here there are at least four.

options.text: Validation, persistence, notification and audit logging are four independently changeable concerns bundled into one method; a change to the welcome email's wording or the audit schema forces an edit to `register`, which has nothing to do with validating or storing a user.
options.explanation: Correct. Each of these four concerns can change for a reason unrelated to the other three, yet all four live inside one method that must be touched whenever any of them changes.

options.text: The class constructs a `User` directly instead of using a factory, which violates SRP because object construction is always a separate responsibility from business logic.
options.explanation: Constructing a small value object inline is not an SRP violation by itself — object creation only becomes a separate concern when it is complex or reused enough to deserve its own class; the real issue here is persistence, email and auditing sharing one method, not the `new User(...)` call.

options.text: Using `jdbcTemplate` ties the class to Spring, which violates SRP because a service class should never depend on a framework type, the same way depending on `SimpleMailMessage` or the `@Service` annotation itself would also count as a forbidden framework dependency under this reading of the principle.
options.explanation: Depending on a framework helper like `JdbcTemplate` is a dependency and testability concern, not an SRP violation; SRP is about how many unrelated reasons to change are mixed together, not which library supplies a collaborator.
